solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Price of a suit? (5)

blocks.note: the surface wants a shop price; the setter means the sum a court orders the loser to pay
the surface wants a suit of clothes; the setter means a lawsuit

annotation.surface: A shopper asks what a new suit will set them back.
annotation.walkthrough: The suit is a lawsuit, not clothing: COSTS are what a court orders the losing side to pay. The question mark flags the second sense.
annotation.definitionFit: Legal costs are the price paid for bringing or losing a suit in court.

entries.clue: Tale about Poe’s visitor’s break (10)

indicatorNotes.about: the tale goes around, or about, the bird

blocks.note: a conte is a short tale
the bird that visits the narrator in Poe's poem The Raven

annotation.surface: A literary note on the story behind the visitor in an Edgar Allan Poe poem.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s stands for 'is' or 'has', linking wordplay to definition. 'Break' is a verb here: to break a rule.
annotation.definitionFit: Contravene is a plain synonym of break in its rule-breaking sense, not the smashing one the surface might suggest.

entries.clue: Costumier using tar to coat a foul string shirt? (6,3,6)

indicatorNotes.to coat: the sailor covers the letters that follow, as a coat covers a body

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor
kept as written
foul = vile
a string of things in a line is a row
T as in T-shirt; the question mark admits the stretch

annotation.surface: A tailor who waterproofs a shirt with tar, which sounds grim.
annotation.walkthrough: Savile Row is the London street famous for bespoke tailoring. The question mark on 'shirt?' admits that only the T of T-shirt is wanted.
annotation.definitionFit: A Savile Row tailor makes suits to measure, so is a maker of costumes in the broad sense.

entries.clue: Island’s top religious schools backed (2,5)

indicatorNotes.backed: sent backwards, so the letters read in reverse

blocks.note: A1 means first-rate, with the 1 read as the letter I
cults are religious sects or schools of belief

annotation.surface: A claim that an island's best church schools have received financial backing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Backed' pretends to mean sponsored; here it means read backwards. Writing A1 as AI is a common crossword trick.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: St Lucia is one particular Caribbean island.

entries.clue: Horse in Shropshire getting around paths of shells (9)

indicatorNotes.in: the horse sits inside the county
indicatorNotes.getting around: the county turns round, reading backwards

blocks.note: Salop is the old name and abbreviation for Shropshire, an English county
an Arab is a breed of horse

annotation.surface: A horse in rural Shropshire picking its way along paths strewn with shells.
annotation.walkthrough: The shells are artillery shells, not seashells: a fired shell follows a parabola. Salop is still used for the county in postal addresses.
annotation.definitionFit: A projectile such as a shell travels along a parabolic curve.

entries.clue: A pretty cold flying animal, long dead (11)

indicatorNotes.flying: the letters take flight and land in a new order

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 11 letters

annotation.surface: Something that was quite chilly as it flew, and has been dead a long time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Flying' does double duty: it stirs the letters and sits in the definition, since the pterodactyl was a flying reptile.
annotation.definitionFit: The pterodactyl was a flying reptile that died out with the dinosaurs.

entries.clue: Fabulous flier from “The Sound of Music”? (3)

indicatorNotes.Sound of: we want what the kind of music sounds like when said

blocks.note: rock is a kind of music

annotation.surface: A fairy-tale bird taken from the musical The Sound of Music.
annotation.walkthrough: The quotation marks dress up the film title; split it and 'Sound of' asks for the sound of a type of music.
annotation.definitionFit: The roc is a giant bird of Arabian legend, a fabulous flier.

entries.clue: Metal that is wood (7)

blocks.note: brass is a metal alloy
i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'

annotation.surface: Someone insisting that a metal is really wood.
annotation.walkthrough: A brassie is an old golf club, a wooden-headed club with a brass sole plate, so the metal and the wood meet in one object.
annotation.definitionFit: Woods are golf clubs, and the brassie is the old name for the 2-wood.

entries.clue: Quickly care for those giving a hand (4,3,8)

blocks.note: to care for someone is to like them
people giving a hand, or a round of applause, are the clappers

annotation.surface: Hurry and look after the people who are helping out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Like the clappers' is British slang for very fast. 'Giving a hand' looks like helping, but it means applauding.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'like the clappers' is British slang for very fast, the clappers being bell tongues swinging hard.

entries.clue: Connection linking Chelsea with Middlesbrough (4)

indicatorNotes.linking: 'linking' joins the end of one name to the start of the other

blocks.note: the last three letters of Chelsea
the first letter of Middlesbrough

annotation.surface: A football link between two English clubs, Chelsea and Middlesbrough.
annotation.walkthrough: The answer sits across the join of the two names, just like a seam between two cloths.
annotation.definitionFit: A seam is the line where two pieces of cloth are joined, a connection in the literal sense.

entries.clue: Still around, nursing sick boy (7)

indicatorNotes.around: the word turns round, reading backwards
indicatorNotes.nursing: holding the sick letters inside, as a nurse holds a patient

blocks.note: still = even, as in 'still better' / 'even better'
sick = ill

annotation.surface: Someone who is still at home looking after a poorly son.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Nursing' and 'sick' make a sickbed picture, but nursing only means holding inside.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Neville is one particular name given to a boy.

entries.clue: Annual prank embraced by spies (7)

indicatorNotes.embraced by: the prank is held inside the spies

blocks.note: the CIA is the US spy agency
a lark is a prank

annotation.surface: A yearly practical joke that the intelligence service goes along with.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Annual' looks like an adjective for the prank, but it is a noun: a plant that lives one year.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: clarkia is one of the garden plants that grow, flower and die within a year, which gardeners call annuals.

entries.clue: Artefact priest found hidden by worshipper (5)

indicatorNotes.found hidden by: the priest is concealed inside the worshipper's letters

blocks.note: RC = Roman Catholic
Eli is the priest who raised Samuel in the Bible

annotation.surface: An old object once belonging to a priest, kept secretly by a churchgoer.
annotation.walkthrough: Eli is the crossword's favourite priest. The religious surface fits the answer, as relics are often holy objects.
annotation.definitionFit: A relic is an object surviving from the past.

entries.clue: Refuse to accept, for example (8)

blocks.note: the surface wants an action, declining to take something; the setter means two words, refuse and accept, set side by side
that pair is an instance of the thing the answer names

annotation.surface: An example of someone declining to take something.
annotation.walkthrough: Read 'Refuse to accept' as a pair of words: refuse to accept, and accept to refuse, each is the other's opposite.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the verbs refuse and accept mean contrary things, and a word of contrary meaning is called an opposite.

entries.clue: For good exercise, put out my lantern (11)

indicatorNotes.put out: the letters are disturbed and put out of order

blocks.note: PE = physical education
anagram of MYLANTERN

annotation.surface: For the sake of the workout, someone is told to extinguish their lamp.
annotation.walkthrough: 'For good' reads as 'for the benefit of', but together it means forever. 'Put out' pretends to mean extinguish.
annotation.definitionFit: Something done for good is done permanently.

entries.clue: Arsenal reserves or those getting treatment (10)

indicatorNotes.reserves: re-serves: the letters are served up again in a new order

blocks.note: anagram of ORTHOSE
the use of something is how it is treated

annotation.surface: A football report on Arsenal's reserve team and its injured players.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is all about the London football club; here an arsenal is a store of weapons. 'Reserves' looks like a noun, but it is the instruction.
annotation.definitionFit: An arsenal in its original sense is a building where weapons are stored; the football club took its name from one.

entries.clue: Contract, it is said (6,9)

blocks.note: a deal made in words rather than writing
'is' agrees with its subject 'it', an agreement of the verb in grammar

annotation.surface: Someone describing a deal as the thing people claim it is.
annotation.walkthrough: 'It is' is an example of a verb agreeing with its subject, which grammarians call verbal agreement. A spoken contract has the same name.
annotation.definitionFit: Verbal agreement covers both senses: a spoken contract, and the grammar rule by which 'it' takes 'is'.

entries.clue: Take-home pay included? I may confuse a hippie (3,3,9)

indicatorNotes.included: the pay is put inside the take-home

blocks.note: net pay is what you take home
pay = wage
one who ravels, or tangles, things up

annotation.surface: Someone wonders whether their pay packet is enough to baffle a hippie.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Take-home pay' reads as one phrase, but it splits in two. A New Age traveller is a British term for a nomadic hippie living in vans or buses.
annotation.definitionFit: New Age travellers are people with hippie values who live on the road.

entries.clue: Giant reached hospital, hiding back trouble (7)

blocks.note: got to = reached
H is the map symbol for hospital
to ail is to trouble

annotation.surface: A giant arrives at hospital, concealing his bad back.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Back trouble' reads as a medical complaint, but 'back' just reverses AIL.
annotation.definitionFit: Goliath is the Philistine giant slain by David.

entries.clue: Finishes posting, site initially down (7)

indicatorNotes.down: in a down entry, the S moves to the bottom

blocks.note: posting a letter is sending it
the first letter of 'site'

annotation.surface: Someone stops putting things online because the website has crashed.
annotation.walkthrough: SENDING starts with S; take that S off and put it at the bottom of the word. 'Down' reads as 'offline'.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the finishes of stories or races are their endings, both plural nouns.

entries.clue: Swiss artist’s UK pal redesigned shelter (4,4)

blocks.note: anagram of UKPAL
the lee is the sheltered side

annotation.surface: A Swiss artist's British friend has redone his shed or shelter.
annotation.walkthrough: The ’s means 'is', linking definition to wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Paul Klee, the Bauhaus painter, was born in Switzerland.

entries.clue: Severity of report from plumber (5)

blocks.note: how serious or profound a crisis is
one who plumbs the water with a weighted line reports how deep it is

annotation.surface: How bad things are, going by what the plumber reports.
annotation.walkthrough: A plumber here is someone who plumbs, sounding the water with a weighted line; what he reports is the depth.
annotation.definitionFit: Depth covers both senses: how serious a crisis is, and the sounding a plumb line gives.

entries.clue: Declare love in a car (4)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' places love physically inside the car, just as a passenger sits in one

blocks.note: a VW, a Volkswagen
love = zero in tennis, the letter O

annotation.surface: Proposing to someone while sitting in a car.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Declare love' reads as a single romantic act, but 'Declare' alone is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to avow a feeling is to declare it openly.

entries.clue: Criminal gets in to rear of house (7)

indicatorNotes.to rear of: IN goes after, at the back of, the house

blocks.note: a villa is a house
kept as written

annotation.surface: A burglar breaks in at the back of a house.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a break-in, and the answer is the burglar.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, and in British slang a villain specifically means a crook.

entries.clue: Head teachers’ association (3)

blocks.note: slang for the skull, as in 'use your loaf'
the National Union of Teachers, a British trade union

annotation.surface: A title for a head teachers' union.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Head teachers' reads as one phrase, but the break comes after 'Head'.
annotation.definitionFit: Nut covers both senses: slang for the skull, and the initials of the National Union of Teachers.

entries.clue: 1000kg gold cover for car (7)

blocks.note: a metric tonne is 1000 kilograms
Au is the chemical symbol for gold

annotation.surface: A ton of gold used to cover a car.
annotation.walkthrough: A tonneau is a cover fitted over the open back of a car or pickup truck.
annotation.definitionFit: A tonneau cover protects the open passenger or load area of a vehicle.

entries.clue: Fret about that which is possible (5,1,3)

indicatorNotes.about: 'about' in its sense of around: worry is wrapped around 'that' on every side

blocks.note: fret = worry
kept as written

annotation.surface: Worrying about what might happen.
annotation.walkthrough: 'That which is possible' reads as one phrase, but 'that' belongs to the wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: Something worth a try is possible enough to attempt.

entries.clue: German might thus say it about American girl (5)

indicatorNotes.about: the German word goes around the American

blocks.note: sie is German for she, and for 'it' when the noun is feminine
US = American

annotation.surface: A German speaker referring to an American girl.
annotation.walkthrough: German nouns have gender, so a German might call a thing 'she', sie, where English says 'it'.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Susie is one particular name given to a girl.
